Part (a)

Write the numWordsOfLength method that returns the count of words with exactly len letters.

Try It First! Attempt to solve this part before viewing the solution. Use the concepts: ArrayList traversal.

Solution

public int numWordsOfLength(int len)
{
    int numWords = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < myList.size(); i++)
    {
        String word = (String) myList.get(i);
        if (word.length() == len)
            numWords++;
    }
    return numWords;
}

Part (b)

Write the removeWordsOfLength method that removes all words with exactly len letters from the list.

Solution

public void removeWordsOfLength(int len)
{
    int i = 0;
    while (i < myList.size())
    {
        String word = (String) myList.get(i);
        if (word.length() == len)
            myList.remove(i);
        else
            i++;
    }
}

Key Concepts

✓ Use a while loop (not for-each) when removing elements to avoid ConcurrentModificationException
✓ Only increment index when NOT removing an element
✓ Cast to String was required in 2004 (modern Java uses generics)

Common Mistakes to Avoid

✗ Using for-each loop when removing elements causes ConcurrentModificationException
✗ Incrementing index after removal causes skipped elements
✗ Off-by-one errors in loop bounds
✗ Forgetting to cast Object to String (2004 requirement)

Part (a)

Write the forwardMoveBlocked method that returns true if the robot cannot move in the direction it's facing.

Try It First! Attempt to solve this part before viewing the solution. Use the concepts: Array traversal.

Solution

private boolean forwardMoveBlocked()
{
    if (facingRight)
        return pos == hall.length - 1;
    else
        return pos == 0;
}

Part (b)

Write the move method that decrements the current position's value and moves the robot according to specified rules.

Solution

private void move()
{
    if (hall[pos] > 0)
        hall[pos]--;
    
    if (hall[pos] == 0)
    {
        if (forwardMoveBlocked())
            facingRight = !facingRight;
        else if (facingRight)
            pos++;
        else
            pos--;
    }
}

Part (c)

Write the clearHall method that repeatedly moves the robot until the hall is clear, returning the number of moves.

Solution

public int clearHall()
{
    int count = 0;
    while (!hallIsClear())
    {
        move();
        count++;
    }
    return count;
}

Key Concepts

✓ Boolean instance variables track robot state
✓ Boundary checking prevents array index errors
✓ Simulation problems require careful state updates
✓ Use helper methods (hallIsClear) even if not implementing them

Common Mistakes to Avoid

✗ Off-by-one errors when checking array bounds
✗ Forgetting to toggle direction with facingRight = !facingRight
✗ Not decrementing hall[pos] before checking if it's zero
✗ Infinite loops if move() doesn't update state correctly

Write the requestRoom method that assigns a guest to the first available room or adds them to the waitlist.

Try It First! Attempt to solve this part before viewing the solution. Use the concepts: Array traversal.

Solution

public Reservation requestRoom(String guestName)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < rooms.length; i++)
    {
        if (rooms[i] == null)
        {
            rooms[i] = new Reservation(guestName, i);
            return rooms[i];
        }
    }
    
    waitList.add(guestName);
    return null;
}

Part (b)

Write the cancelAndReassign method that cancels a reservation and assigns the room to the first person on the waitlist.

Solution

public Reservation cancelAndReassign(Reservation res)
{
    int index = res.getRoomNumber();
    
    if (waitList.size() > 0)
    {
        String guestName = (String) waitList.remove(0);
        rooms[index] = new Reservation(guestName, index);
    }
    else
    {
        rooms[index] = null;
    }
    
    return rooms[index];
}

Key Concepts

✓ null represents an empty room in the array
✓ ArrayList.remove(0) removes and returns the first element
✓ Create new Reservation objects with constructor
✓ Return null when no room is available

Common Mistakes to Avoid

✗ Forgetting to check if waitList is empty before removing
✗ Not setting rooms[index] to null when no one is waiting
✗ Returning the wrong value (old vs new reservation)
✗ Index errors when accessing the rooms array

Part (a)

Write the average method that calculates the arithmetic mean of scores between indices first and last (inclusive).

Try It First! Attempt to solve this part before viewing the solution. Use the concepts: Array traversal.

Solution

private double average(int first, int last)
{
    int sum = 0;
    int numScores = 0;
    
    for (int i = first; i <= last; i++)
    {
        sum += scores[i];
        numScores++;
    }
    
    return sum / (double) numScores;
}

Part (b)

Write the hasImproved method that returns true if each score is greater than or equal to the previous score.

Solution

private boolean hasImproved()
{
    for (int i = 1; i < scores.length; i++)
    {
        if (scores[i] < scores[i - 1])
            return false;
    }
    return true;
}

Part (c)

Write the finalAverage method that returns the average of all scores, or just the second half if the student improved.

Solution

public double finalAverage()
{
    int start = 0;
    
    if (hasImproved())
        start = scores.length / 2;
    
    return average(start, scores.length - 1);
}

Key Concepts

✓ Cast to double to avoid integer division truncation
✓ Use i <= last for inclusive bounds
✓ Method composition: finalAverage calls hasImproved and average
✓ scores.length / 2 gives the midpoint index

Common Mistakes to Avoid

✗ Integer division: sum / numScores loses decimal precision
✗ Off-by-one: using i < last instead of i <= last
✗ Comparing wrong indices in hasImproved
✗ Not using the helper methods in finalAverage

Part (a)

Write the conflictsWith method that returns true if this appointment's time overlaps with another appointment's time.

Try It First! Attempt to solve this part before viewing the solution.

Solution

public boolean conflictsWith(Appointment other)
{
    return getTime().overlapsWith(other.getTime());
}

Part (b)

Write the clearConflicts method that removes all appointments from the schedule that conflict with the given appointment.

Solution

public void clearConflicts(Appointment appt)
{
    int i = 0;
    
    while (i < apptList.size())
    {
        Appointment listAppt = (Appointment) apptList.get(i);
        if (appt.conflictsWith(listAppt))
            apptList.remove(i);
        else
            i++;
    }
}

Part (c)

Write the addAppt method that adds an appointment to the schedule, clearing conflicts first if it's an emergency.

Solution

public boolean addAppt(Appointment appt, boolean emergency)
{
    if (emergency)
    {
        clearConflicts(appt);
        apptList.add(appt);
        return true;
    }
    
    for (int i = 0; i < apptList.size(); i++)
    {
        Appointment listAppt = (Appointment) apptList.get(i);
        if (appt.conflictsWith(listAppt))
            return false;
    }
    
    apptList.add(appt);
    return true;
}

Key Concepts

✓ Use helper methods (conflictsWith) when they're provided
✓ While loop for removal prevents skipping elements
✓ Only increment index when NOT removing
✓ Check emergency flag first for early return pattern

Common Mistakes to Avoid

✗ Using for-each loop when removing causes ConcurrentModificationException
✗ Incrementing index after removal skips elements
✗ Not using the provided conflictsWith method
✗ Forgetting to add the appointment after clearing conflicts

Try It First! Attempt to solve this part before viewing the solution.

Solution

public static boolean isSelfDivisor(int number)
{
    int numRemaining = number;
    
    while (numRemaining > 0)
    {
        int digit = numRemaining % 10;
        
        if (digit == 0 || number % digit != 0)
            return false;
        
        numRemaining /= 10;
    }
    
    return true;
}

Part (b)

Write the firstNumSelfDivisors method that returns an array of the first n self-divisors starting from a given value.

public static int[] firstNumSelfDivisors(int start, int num)
{
    int[] selfDivisors = new int[num];
    int count = 0;
    int current = start;
    
    while (count < num)
    {
        if (isSelfDivisor(current))
        {
            selfDivisors[count] = current;
            count++;
        }
        current++;
    }
    
    return selfDivisors;
}

✓ Check for 0 digit first to avoid division by zero

public static int getLongestRun(int[] values)
{
    int maxRunStart = -1;
    int maxRunLength = 0;
    int currentStart = 0;
    int currentLength = 1;
    
    for (int i = 1; i < values.length; i++)
    {
        if (values[i] == values[i - 1])
        {
            currentLength++;
        }
        else
        {
            if (currentLength > 1 && currentLength > maxRunLength)
            {
                maxRunStart = currentStart;
                maxRunLength = currentLength;
            }
            currentStart = i;
            currentLength = 1;
        }
    }
    
    // Check last run
    if (currentLength > 1 && currentLength > maxRunLength)
    {
        maxRunStart = currentStart;
    }
    
    return maxRunStart;
}

        {
            if (index < str.length())

public String encryptMessage(String message)
{
    String result = "";
    fillBlock(message);
    
    for (int c = 0; c < numCols; c++)
    {
        for (int r = 0; r < numRows; r++)
        {
            result += letterBlock[r][c];
        }
    }
    return result;
}

{
    view = new double[numRows][numCols];
    int index = 0;
    
    for (int r = 0; r < numRows; r++)
    {
        if (r % 2 == 0)
        {
            for (int c = 0; c < numCols; c++)

                view[r][c] = scanned[index];

    for (int r = startRow; r <= endRow; r++)
    {
        for (int c = startCol; c <= endCol; c++)
        {
            sum += view[r][c];
            count++;
        }
    }
    return sum / count;
}

AP Computer Science A – Complete AP Exam Review (2025)

This comprehensive AP CSA Exam Review will help you understand the exam format, master MCQs and FRQs, eliminate common mistakes, and adopt high-performing strategies used by students who consistently earn 4s and 5s.

📘 5.1 What the AP CSA Exam Actually Tests

The AP Computer Science A exam measures your ability to think, reason, trace, and design programs using object-oriented programming in Java. Contrary to what many students think, the exam does not reward memorization. Instead, the AP exam tests:

  • Logical reasoning and tracing ability
  • Understanding Java behavior (especially object references)
  • Ability to analyze and modify existing code
  • Correct use of arrays and ArrayLists
  • Proper class construction: constructors, methods, fields
  • Control structures: loops and selection
  • Recognizing errors and edge cases

You do not need to memorize:

  • Java libraries beyond what’s required (no HashMaps, no file I/O)
  • Complex algorithms (merge sort, binary search)
  • Java syntax obscure features
The strongest students don’t memorize—they understand patterns. The AP CSA exam tests habits of thinking more than raw knowledge.

📝 5.2 AP CSA Exam Format (2025 Update)

As of the current AP Computer Science A exam specification, the exam is structured as follows:

📌 Section I — Multiple Choice (MCQ)

  • 40 questions
  • 90 minutes
  • 50% of your exam score
  • Single-select, no penalty for guessing
  • Covers Units 1–4, with heavy emphasis on Unit 4

📌 Section II — Free Response (FRQ)

  • 4 FRQs
  • 90 minutes
  • 50% of exam score
  • All require writing Java code by hand
  • The 4 FRQ types are typically:
    • Methods & Control Structures
    • Class Design
    • Array / Array Algorithm
    • ArrayList / Data Structure
FRQ #2 and FRQ #4 almost always relate to Unit 4: Data Collections. This means mastering arrays and ArrayLists gives you a huge scoring advantage.

🎯 5.3 How to Study for AP CSA (Most Effective Strategy)

Students often waste hours “practicing Java” without learning what the AP exam actually wants. The following approach is the most efficient and proven way to prepare for the test.

Step 1 — Master Tracing

Tracing means following code line-by-line and predicting the output or final state. Over half of the MCQs are tracing-based.

x = 3 for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { x += i; } // x → 3+0 → 3+1 → 3+2 = 6

Step 2 — Memorize Common Patterns, Not Syntax

  • sum/count loops
  • max/min loops
  • index-based traversal of arrays
  • removal pattern for ArrayLists
  • constructor + getter + setter trio

Step 3 — Practice FRQ Structure

Most FRQ points come from clean structure: correct headers, correct return types, and proper use of instance variables—not fancy code.

Step 4 — Do Actual Practice Exams

Nothing replaces real AP-style practice. Use:

  • Your own practice exams (on your site)

🔁 5.4 MCQ Strategy — How to Increase Your Score Quickly

The multiple-choice section rewards pattern recognition and precision. These are the most effective MCQ strategies:

Tip 1 — Always Identify the Topic First

Before looking at the answer choices, identify whether the question is testing:

  • Array traversal
  • ArrayList shifting
  • Object references
  • Boolean logic
  • Constructor behavior
  • Loop conditions

Tip 2 — Predict the Answer Before Reading Choices

This prevents you from being “persuaded” by tricky distractors.

Tip 3 — Draw Quick Diagrams

Especially for array index movement, ArrayList shifts, and reference tracing.

Tip 4 — When Unsure, Eliminate Wrong Answers Fast

You can almost always eliminate:

  • Choices involving impossible index values
  • Choices that violate Java syntax
  • Choices contradicting loop behavior

Tip 5 — Don’t Overthink Easy Questions

The AP includes many straightforward tracing and array questions—don’t assume they’re trick questions.

Good MCQ performance comes from recognizing patterns, not being a “Java expert.”

🏗 5.5 FRQ Strategy — How to Guarantee Points

FRQs are where students can earn huge gains because graders reward structure and correctness, not elegance. You can often score 7/9 points on an FRQ without writing flawless code.

FRQ Scoring Reality

  • Each FRQ is scored on a rubric with 9 points.
  • Most points come from:
    • correct method headers

🧠 5.6 Deep-Dive FRQ Strategy: How to Write Code Under Pressure

Performing well on the FRQs isn’t about writing perfect Java—it’s about showing the grader you understand logic, structure, and reasoning. Here is the most reliable method for scoring high.

1. Start With the Method Header

You earn points instantly for writing a correct method signature:

public int countGreaterThan(int[] arr, int value)
You don’t need to understand the whole problem—write the header first.

2. Write the Loop Structure Next

All array/ArrayList FRQs rely on this skeleton:

for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) {
    // logic here
}

3. Use Instance Variables Properly

If the FRQ gives you fields like:

private int count;
private ArrayList words;

Never redeclare them inside the method. Use this.count or words.get(i).

4. Always Handle Edge Cases

Many FRQ points are awarded for avoiding errors like:

  • index out of bounds
  • null or empty arrays
  • checking size before removing items

5. Return Something Even if Unsure

A missing return statement loses guaranteed points. Even a wrong return value earns partial credit if structure is correct.

FRQ grading is generous. If your code is “logically on the right track,” you can score 7–8/9 points.

⚠️ 5.8 The Most Common Mistakes on the AP CSA Exam

1. Off-by-One Errors

60% of students lose points for missing one index. Always verify your loop boundaries:

  • Arrays → i < arr.length
  • ArrayLists → i < list.size()

2. Confusing == with equals()

== compares memory references. equals() compares String content.

3. Calling Methods Incorrectly

Remember: instance methods need an object:

word.toUpperCase();

4. Invalid Removal from ArrayLists

Use a while loop with index control when removing items:

int i = 0;
while (i < list.size()) {
    if (list.get(i) < 0) {
        list.remove(i);
    } else {
        i++;
    }
}

5. Forgetting Return Statements

1 missing return = immediate point loss. Always return something—even a placeholder.

<h2>What is an algorithm, and what does a computer do with it?</h2>
<p>
  Every time you follow a recipe, give someone directions to your house, or work through long division, you are running an algorithm. You start with an input, you follow a fixed sequence of steps, and you end up with a result. Computer science takes that same everyday idea and asks a tighter question: what is the precise, unambiguous list of steps that solves this problem, and how do we hand those steps to a machine that has zero common sense?
</p>

<div class="apcsa-callout concept">
  <h4>Definition</h4>
  <p>An <strong>algorithm</strong> is a step-by-step process for completing a task or solving a problem. Algorithms can be represented in written language, in diagrams (like flowcharts), or in a programming language. <strong>Sequencing</strong> is the part of an algorithm that defines the order in which steps are performed, one step at a time.</p>
</div>

<p>
  AP CSA is, at its core, a course about writing algorithms in Java. Before any code is involved, though, the algorithm has to exist as a clear, ordered plan. The CED is explicit about this: students should be able to <em>represent patterns and algorithms found in everyday life</em>, not just type Java. The reason is practical. Programmers who can’t describe their plan in plain English usually can’t describe it in Java either. They end up debugging a mental model that was never coherent to begin with.
</p>

<h3>Sequencing: one step at a time, in a specific order</h3>
<p>
  Sequencing sounds obvious until you try to break it. Consider making a peanut butter sandwich. “Spread the peanut butter, take out the bread, open the jar” lists all the right ingredients but produces a mess. The same is true in code. <code>System.out.println(name); String name = "Tanner";</code> uses the right pieces but compiles only if reordered. Computers execute statements <strong>one at a time, in the order written</strong>, with no ability to look ahead or guess what you meant.
</p>

<div class="apcsa-callout example">
  <h4>Example</h4>
  <p>Algorithm for “log in to a website”: (1) open the login page, (2) type the username, (3) type the password, (4) click submit, (5) wait for the server response, (6) display the home page <em>only if</em> the response was successful. Swap steps 3 and 4 and the password is never entered. Swap steps 4 and 5 and the user clicks submit before there’s anything to submit. The steps haven’t changed; only the sequence has, and the sequence is what makes it work.</p>
</div>

<h3>From algorithm to running program: writing, compiling, executing</h3>
<p>
  Once you have an algorithm, you write it in a programming language. Java code can be written in any text editor, but most programmers use an <strong>integrated development environment (IDE)</strong>, a single application that lets you write the code, compile it, and run it without leaving the window. Common AP CSA classroom IDEs include IntelliJ IDEA, Eclipse, BlueJ, and Replit. The CED treats the choice of IDE as classroom-dependent and not tested directly, what <em>is</em> tested is what the IDE does for you.
</p>
<p>
  The key step is <strong>compilation</strong>. A <strong>compiler</strong> is a program that translates your Java source code into a form the machine can run, and along the way it checks the code for certain kinds of errors. If the compiler finds an error, your program does not run at all. You must fix the error first. This is one of the most important ideas in this lesson: <em>the compiler is a gatekeeper for one class of mistakes, but it is blind to others</em>.
</p>

<div class="apcsa-callout warning">
  <h4>Common misconception</h4>
  <p>“If my code compiles, it works.” This is wrong, and the AP exam tests it directly. The compiler only catches errors related to the rules of the Java language (missing semicolons, undeclared variables, type mismatches). A program can compile cleanly, run end-to-end, and still produce the wrong answer because the <em>logic</em>, the algorithm you wrote, is flawed. Successful compilation means “Java accepts this as valid Java,” not “this solves your problem.”</p>
</div>

<h3>The four error types you must distinguish</h3>
<p>
  The CED is unusually specific here. Topic 1.1.C names four error categories, and the AP exam tests whether you can place a given mistake into the right bucket. The distinctions matter because they tell you <em>when</em> an error will surface: at compile time, at run time, or only when you happen to test with the right input.
</p>
<ul>
  <li>A <strong>syntax error</strong> is a violation of the rules of the Java language. Missing semicolon, misspelled keyword, unclosed brace. The compiler catches every syntax error. Your program does not run.</li>
  <li>A <strong>logic error</strong> is a mistake in the algorithm itself. The code compiles and runs but produces wrong output. You only catch logic errors by testing with specific inputs and comparing actual output to expected output.</li>
  <li>A <strong>run-time error</strong> is a problem that occurs <em>during execution</em>. The compiler accepted the code, but something goes wrong while the program is running, usually causing it to terminate abnormally.</li>
  <li>An <strong>exception</strong> is a specific type of run-time error: an unexpected condition that the compiler couldn’t predict, which interrupts the normal flow of execution. <code>ArithmeticException</code> from dividing by zero and <code>NullPointerException</code> from calling a method on <code>null</code> are the two you’ll see most often in Unit 1.</li>
</ul>

<div class="apcsa-callout key-insight">
  <h4>Key insight</h4>
  <p>The compiler catches <em>syntax</em> errors only. Logic, run-time, and exception errors all slip past the compiler. They require running the program (and often testing with specific inputs) to surface. This is why writing test cases is part of programming, not an optional extra.</p>
</div>

<td>A step-by-step process for completing a task or solving a problem, representable in written language, diagrams, or code.</td>

<script>
(function(){
  'use strict';

  var nativeFetch = window.__nativeFetch || window.fetch.bind(window);
  var PROXY_URL = 'https://progress.apcsexamprep.com/api/judge0/run';
  var CSACE_RUNS = 0, CSACE_RUN_CAP = 60, CSACE_COOLDOWN_MS = 3000;

  var CSACE_PROBLEMS = [
  {
    id: 'p1',
    title: 'Problem 1 of 3 — spot the compile error',
    prompt: 'This should print <code>Hello, AP CSA</code> but will not compile. Fix it so it runs.',
    starter: `public class Main
{
    public static void main(String[] args)
    {
        System.out.println("Hello, AP CSA")
    }
}`,
    expected: `Hello, AP CSA`,
    hint: 'Every Java statement ends with the same punctuation mark. Read the print line all the way to the end.'
  },
  {
    id: 'p2',
    title: 'Problem 2 of 3 — fix the bug',
    prompt: 'A program runs steps in order. This should print <code>First</code> then <code>Second</code>, but the lines come out reversed. Fix the order.',
    starter: `public class Main
{
    public static void main(String[] args)
    {
        System.out.println("Second");
        System.out.println("First");
    }
}`,
    expected: `First
Second`,
    hint: 'Statements run top to bottom, in the order you write them. Which line does the expected output show first?'
  },
  {
    id: 'p3',
    title: 'Problem 3 of 3 — write from spec',
    prompt: 'Write code that prints exactly two lines: <code>Algorithm</code> on the first line and <code>Program</code> on the second.',
    starter: `public class Main
{
    public static void main(String[] args)
    {
        // print Algorithm, then Program, each on its own line

    }
}`,
    expected: `Algorithm
Program`,
    hint: 'Each print-line statement puts its output on its own line. How many lines does the expected output have, and so how many statements do you need?'
  }
];

  var editors = {};

  function normalize(s) {
    if (!s) {
      return '';
    }
    return s.replace(/\r\n/g, '\n').split('\n').map(function(line){
      return line.replace(/\s+$/, '');
    }).join('\n').replace(/\n+$/, '');
  }

  function el(tag, cls, html) {
    var node = document.createElement(tag);
    if (cls) {
      node.className = cls;
    }
    if (html !== undefined) {
      node.innerHTML = html;
    }
    return node;
  }

  function buildProblem(p, idx) {
    var card = el('div', 'csa-ce-problem');
    card.appendChild(el('div', 'csa-ce-num', p.title));
    card.appendChild(el('div', 'csa-ce-prompt', p.prompt));

    var edWrap = el('div', 'csa-ce-editor');
    var ta = document.createElement('textarea');
    ta.value = p.starter;
    edWrap.appendChild(ta);
    card.appendChild(edWrap);

    var row = el('div', 'csa-ce-btnrow');
    var runBtn = el('button', 'csa-ce-run', 'Run ▶');
    var hintBtn = el('button', 'csa-ce-hintbtn', 'Hint');
    var resetBtn = el('button', 'csa-ce-resetbtn', 'Reset');
    var wrapBtn = el('button', 'csa-ce-wrapbtn', 'Wrap lines');
    var status = el('span', 'csa-ce-status', '');
    row.appendChild(runBtn);
    row.appendChild(hintBtn);
    row.appendChild(resetBtn);
    row.appendChild(wrapBtn);
    row.appendChild(status);
    card.appendChild(row);

    var out = el('div', 'csa-ce-output');
    card.appendChild(out);

    var hint = el('div', 'csa-ce-hint', '💡 ' + p.hint);
    card.appendChild(hint);

    document.getElementById('csa-ce-problems').appendChild(card);

    var cm = CodeMirror.fromTextArea(ta, {
      mode: 'text/x-java',
      lineNumbers: true,
      indentUnit: 4,
      tabSize: 4,
      indentWithTabs: false,
      viewportMargin: Infinity,
      lineWrapping: (window.innerWidth <= 600)
    });
    editors[p.id] = cm;
    setTimeout(function(){ cm.refresh(); }, 0);
    setTimeout(function(){ cm.refresh(); }, 350);

    hintBtn.onclick = function() {
      hint.classList.toggle('show');
    };

    if (cm.getOption('lineWrapping')) { wrapBtn.className = 'csa-ce-wrapbtn on'; wrapBtn.innerHTML = 'Wrap: on'; }
    wrapBtn.onclick = function() {
      var on = !cm.getOption('lineWrapping');
      cm.setOption('lineWrapping', on);
      wrapBtn.className = on ? 'csa-ce-wrapbtn on' : 'csa-ce-wrapbtn';
      wrapBtn.innerHTML = on ? 'Wrap: on' : 'Wrap lines';
      cm.refresh();
    };

    resetBtn.onclick = function() {
      cm.setValue(p.starter);
      out.className = 'csa-ce-output';
      out.textContent = '';
    };

    runBtn.onclick = function() {
      var code = cm.getValue();
      var wrap = document.getElementById('csa-ce-wrap');
      var lessonId = wrap ? (wrap.getAttribute('data-lesson-id') || '') : '';
      if (CSACE_RUNS >= CSACE_RUN_CAP) {
        out.className = 'csa-ce-output show err';
        out.textContent = 'Run limit reached for this page. Refresh to keep practicing.';
        return;
      }
      CSACE_RUNS++;
      runBtn.disabled = true;
      status.textContent = 'Compiling and running...';
      out.className = 'csa-ce-output';
      out.textContent = '';

      nativeFetch(PROXY_URL, {
        method: 'POST',
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
        body: JSON.stringify({ code: code, lessonId: lessonId, problemId: p.id })
      })
      .then(function(res) {
        return res.json().then(function(data) {
          return { ok: res.ok, status: res.status, data: data };
        });
      })
      .then(function(result) {
        setTimeout(function(){ runBtn.disabled = false; }, CSACE_COOLDOWN_MS);
        status.textContent = '';
        var data = result.data;

        if (!result.ok) {
          out.className = 'csa-ce-output show err';
          out.textContent = data.message || 'Run failed. Try again.';
          return;
        }

        if (data.compile_output) {
          out.className = 'csa-ce-output show err';
          out.textContent = 'Compile error:\n' + data.compile_output;
          return;
        }

        if (data.stderr) {
          out.className = 'csa-ce-output show err';
          out.textContent = 'Runtime error:\n' + data.stderr;
          return;
        }

        var stdout = data.stdout || '';

        if (p.expected === null || p.expected === undefined) {
          out.className = 'csa-ce-output show plain';
          out.textContent = 'Output:\n' + (stdout || '(no output)');
          return;
        }

        if (normalize(stdout) === normalize(p.expected)) {
          out.className = 'csa-ce-output show ok';
          if (window.APCS_reportAttempt) { APCS_reportAttempt({ item_id: lessonId + '-code-1', item_type: 'cfu', score: 1, max_score: 1, detail: [{ q: idx + 1, sel: null, ok: true }] }); }
          out.textContent = '✓ Correct!\nOutput: ' + stdout.replace(/\n$/, '');
        } else {
          out.className = 'csa-ce-output show err';
          out.textContent = '✗ Not quite.\nYour output: ' + (stdout.replace(/\n$/, '') || '(none)') + '\nExpected: ' + p.expected;
        }
      })
      .catch(function(err) {
        setTimeout(function(){ runBtn.disabled = false; }, CSACE_COOLDOWN_MS);
        status.textContent = '';
        out.className = 'csa-ce-output show err';
        out.textContent = 'Could not reach the code runner. Check your connection and try again.';
      });
    };
  }

  function init() {
    for (var i = 0; i < CSACE_PROBLEMS.length; i++) {
      buildProblem(CSACE_PROBLEMS[i], i);
    }
  }

  if (document.readyState === 'loading') {
    document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', init);
  } else {
    init();
  }
})();
</script>

<section class="apcsa-practice-tier">
  <h2>
<span class="tier-label">Tier 2 Practice</span> Check your understanding</h2>
  <p style="font-size: 15px !important; color: #475569 !important; -webkit-text-fill-color: #475569 !important;">
    Six questions covering the lesson concepts. On tougher questions, try predicting your answer before reading the options, it’s the best way to catch trap distractors. Mix of formats: MCQ, matching, classification, and a vocabulary cloze.
  </p>

  <!-- EX 1: I/II/III multi-correct, answer C -->
  <div class="apcs-ex" data-type="mcq" data-answer="C" data-item-id="1.1-cfu-1">
    <span class="apcs-ex-label">MCQ · Multi-select stem</span>
    <div class="apcs-ex-stem">
      <strong>1.</strong> A student is writing an algorithm to make oatmeal. Consider the following statements about algorithms and sequencing.
      <ol style="margin-top: 10px !important; padding-left: 24px !important;">
        <li>An algorithm can be represented in written language, in a diagram, or in code, and the representation does not change whether the algorithm is correct.</li>
        <li>Reordering two steps in an algorithm always produces a different result.</li>
        <li>An algorithm only counts as “an algorithm” once it is written in a programming language; a recipe on paper does not qualify.</li>
      </ol>
      Which of the statements are true?
    </div>
    <div class="apcs-ex-options">
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="A">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">A.</span> I only</div>
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="B">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">B.</span> I and II</div>
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="C">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">C.</span> I only is fully correct; II and III are false</div>
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="D">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">D.</span> II and III</div>
    </div>
    <button class="apcs-btn apcs-ex-check">Check answer</button>
    <div class="apcs-ex-feedback">
      <strong>C.</strong> Only statement I is true: the CED explicitly says algorithms can be represented in written language, diagrams, or code, and correctness is independent of representation. Statement II overreaches, reordering two steps <em>can</em> change the result, but if the two steps are independent (e.g., “put on left sock” then “put on right sock”) the result is identical. Statement III is the most common student mistake: a paper recipe and a flowchart are perfectly valid algorithm representations, nothing about the definition requires code.
    </div>
  </div>

  <!-- EX 2: NOT/EXCEPT spot the misconception, predict-gate ON, answer D -->
  <div class="apcs-ex" data-type="mcq" data-answer="D" data-item-id="1.1-cfu-2">
    <span class="apcs-ex-label">MCQ · Spot the misconception</span>
    <div class="apcs-ex-stem">
      <strong>2.</strong> Which of the following statements about compilers and errors is <strong>NOT</strong> true?
    </div>
    <div class="apcs-predict-gate">This stem uses <strong>NOT</strong>. You’re looking for the option that is <em>wrong</em>. Before reading the choices, predict what a compiler can and cannot catch. Then read all four.</div>
    <div class="apcs-ex-options">
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="A">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">A.</span> A program that fails to compile will not run at all until the errors are fixed.</div>
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="B">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">B.</span> Syntax errors are violations of the rules of the programming language and are detected by the compiler.</div>
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="C">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">C.</span> A program can compile successfully and still produce incorrect output for some inputs.</div>
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="D">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">D.</span> If a program compiles successfully, then it will never throw a run-time exception during execution.</div>
    </div>
    <button class="apcs-btn apcs-ex-check">Check answer</button>
    <div class="apcs-ex-feedback">
      <strong>D.</strong> Option D is the false statement, successful compilation means only that the code follows Java’s language rules, not that it is safe at run time. A compiled program can still throw exceptions like <code>ArithmeticException</code> (division by zero) or <code>NullPointerException</code> the moment it tries an operation the compiler couldn’t predict. A, B, and C are all accurate: compile failures block execution, syntax errors are language-rule violations the compiler catches, and clean compilation says nothing about logical correctness.
    </div>
  </div>

  <!-- EX 3: Matching -->
  <div class="apcs-ex" data-type="matching" data-item-id="1.1-cfu-3">
    <span class="apcs-ex-label">Matching</span>
    <div class="apcs-ex-stem">
      <strong>3.</strong> Match each error type on the left to its precise definition on the right.
    </div>
    <div class="apcs-matching">
      <div class="apcs-match-col">
        <div class="apcs-match-item" data-key="t1"><strong>Syntax error</strong></div>
        <div class="apcs-match-item" data-key="t2"><strong>Logic error</strong></div>
        <div class="apcs-match-item" data-key="t3"><strong>Run-time error</strong></div>
        <div class="apcs-match-item" data-key="t4"><strong>Exception</strong></div>
      </div>
      <div class="apcs-match-col">
        <div class="apcs-match-item" data-match="t3">An error that occurs during program execution, typically causing the program to terminate abnormally.</div>
        <div class="apcs-match-item" data-match="t1">A violation of the rules of the programming language; detected by the compiler before the program runs.</div>
        <div class="apcs-match-item" data-match="t4">A type of run-time error from an unexpected condition the compiler did not detect, interrupting normal flow.</div>
        <div class="apcs-match-item" data-match="t2">A mistake in the algorithm itself; the program runs but produces incorrect or unexpected results.</div>
      </div>
    </div>
    <button class="apcs-btn apcs-ex-check">Check matches</button>
    <div class="apcs-ex-feedback">
      Syntax errors live entirely at compile time. Logic errors run cleanly but give wrong answers (think: off-by-one bug in a loop). Run-time errors halt execution mid-program. Exceptions are the specific subset of run-time errors that occur because of unexpected conditions like dividing by zero, every exception is a run-time error, but not every run-time error is an exception.
    </div>
  </div>

  <!-- EX 4: Scenario sort (3 buckets: syntax / logic / run-time) -->
  <div class="apcs-ex" data-type="scenario-sort" data-item-id="1.1-cfu-4">
    <span class="apcs-ex-label">Classify</span>
    <div class="apcs-ex-stem">
      <strong>4.</strong> For each scenario below, classify the error as a syntax error, a logic error, or a run-time error.
    </div>
    <div class="apcs-sort-bank">
      <div class="apcs-sort-item" data-bucket="b1">A student forgets the semicolon at the end of <code>int x = 5</code> and the program will not compile.</div>
      <div class="apcs-sort-item" data-bucket="b2">A program that computes the average of three test scores returns the sum instead because the student forgot to divide by 3.</div>
      <div class="apcs-sort-item" data-bucket="b3">A program crashes with <code>ArithmeticException</code> when the user enters 0 as the divisor.</div>
      <div class="apcs-sort-item" data-bucket="b1">A student types <code>Sytem.out.println</code> with a misspelled class name and the IDE underlines it in red before running.</div>
      <div class="apcs-sort-item" data-bucket="b2">A loop intended to print numbers 1 through 10 prints 0 through 9 because the student started the counter at the wrong value.</div>
      <div class="apcs-sort-item" data-bucket="b3">A program that reads a file crashes partway through with <code>NullPointerException</code> the first time it encounters an empty line.</div>
    </div>
    <div class="apcs-sort-buckets">
      <div class="apcs-sort-bucket" data-bucket="b1"><h5>Syntax error</h5></div>
      <div class="apcs-sort-bucket" data-bucket="b2"><h5>Logic error</h5></div>
      <div class="apcs-sort-bucket" data-bucket="b3"><h5>Run-time error</h5></div>
    </div>
    <button class="apcs-btn apcs-ex-check">Check sorting</button>
    <div class="apcs-ex-feedback">
      The two syntax errors (missing semicolon, misspelled <code>System</code>) are caught by the compiler, so the program never runs. The two logic errors compile and run but produce wrong output: in both cases Java did exactly what was written, which wasn’t what the student meant. The two run-time errors (division by zero, null pointer) compile cleanly and execute until they hit a condition the compiler couldn’t predict.
    </div>
  </div>

  <!-- EX 5: Cloze -->
  <div class="apcs-ex" data-type="cloze" data-item-id="1.1-cfu-5">
    <span class="apcs-ex-label">Cloze · Vocabulary in context</span>
    <div class="apcs-ex-stem">
      <strong>5.</strong> Fill each blank with the correct term from the bank below.
    </div>
    <div class="apcs-cloze-text">
      A student writes a Java program in their
      <span class="apcs-cloze-blank" data-answer="IDE"></span>,
      saves the file, and clicks Run. The
      <span class="apcs-cloze-blank" data-answer="compiler"></span>
      reports no errors, so the program starts executing. After thirty seconds it terminates abnormally with a stack trace; this is a
      <span class="apcs-cloze-blank" data-answer="run-time error"></span>.
      The student fixes the crash, runs the program again, and this time it finishes cleanly but produces the wrong answer for several inputs. This second problem is a
      <span class="apcs-cloze-blank" data-answer="logic error"></span>.
    </div>
    <div class="apcs-cloze-chips">
      <span class="apcs-sort-item" data-term="IDE">IDE</span>
      <span class="apcs-sort-item" data-term="compiler">compiler</span>
      <span class="apcs-sort-item" data-term="run-time error">run-time error</span>
      <span class="apcs-sort-item" data-term="logic error">logic error</span>
      <span class="apcs-sort-item" data-term="syntax error">syntax error</span>
      <span class="apcs-sort-item" data-term="algorithm">algorithm</span>
    </div>
    <button class="apcs-btn apcs-ex-check">Check answers</button>
    <div class="apcs-ex-feedback">
      The IDE is where code is written and managed. The compiler is the gatekeeper before execution; if it reports no errors, syntax is not the problem. A program that compiles but terminates abnormally during execution is hitting a run-time error. A program that compiles, runs to completion, and produces wrong output has a logic error. The algorithm itself is flawed.
    </div>
  </div>

  <!-- EX 6: Applied scenario, answer A -->
  <div class="apcs-ex" data-type="mcq" data-answer="A" data-item-id="1.1-cfu-6">
    <span class="apcs-ex-label">MCQ · Applied scenario</span>
    <div class="apcs-ex-stem">
      <strong>6.</strong> A student writes a Java program that calculates a tip on a restaurant bill. The program compiles without any errors and runs to completion every time, but the tip amount is consistently 10 times larger than it should be. Which of the following best classifies this mistake?
    </div>
    <div class="apcs-ex-options">
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="A">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">A.</span> A logic error, because the program runs without crashing but produces an incorrect result.</div>
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="B">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">B.</span> A syntax error, because the program is using the wrong math operator and the compiler should have caught it.</div>
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="C">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">C.</span> A run-time error, because the wrong value appears during execution rather than at compile time.</div>
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="D">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">D.</span> An exception, because the output deviates from what was expected.</div>
    </div>
    <button class="apcs-btn apcs-ex-check">Check answer</button>
    <div class="apcs-ex-feedback">
      <strong>A.</strong> The defining feature here is that the program compiles, runs to completion, and produces incorrect output, and that is the textbook signature of a logic error. B is wrong because the compiler does not check whether math is “correct” for your purposes; multiplying by 10 instead of 0.1 is valid Java. C is the most attractive trap: a run-time error specifically means execution is interrupted (the program terminates abnormally), which is not what happened. D is wrong because an exception is a specific kind of run-time error, not a generic label for any incorrect output.
    </div>
  </div>

</section>

<section class="apcsa-mastery" data-item-id="1.1-quiz">
  <span class="mastery-badge">Tier 3 · AP Mastery Challenge</span>
  <h2>The After-School Tutoring Scheduler</h2>
  <p>Mr. Ramirez asks two of his students, Sara and Jordan, to write a Java program that prints the names of every student signed up for after-school tutoring on a given day. The program reads names from a text file (one name per line) and prints them in the order they appear. Sara writes the program in IntelliJ, clicks Run, and IntelliJ refuses to start the program; it underlines the second-to-last line in red. Sara fixes the underline and clicks Run again; this time the program starts, prints six names, and then terminates abnormally with a message about <code>NullPointerException</code>. Jordan looks at the same file and notices that the file has an empty line in the middle, which is where Sara’s program crashed. Jordan rewrites the program so it skips empty lines. It now runs to completion. But Mr. Ramirez points out that one of the printed names is wrong: the program is printing every name twice.</p>

  <h3>Part A: Identify Sara’s first error</h3>
  <div class="apcs-ex" data-type="mcq" data-answer="B">
    <div class="apcs-ex-stem">When IntelliJ refused to start Sara’s program and underlined a line in red, what kind of error was Sara hitting?</div>
    <div class="apcs-predict-gate">Predict first: what is the only error type that prevents a program from running at all? Then read the options.</div>
    <div class="apcs-ex-options">
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="A">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">A.</span> A logic error, because the program is producing the wrong result.</div>
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="B">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">B.</span> A syntax error, because the compiler refused to compile the code and flagged a specific line.</div>
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="C">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">C.</span> A run-time error, because the IDE detected it before execution.</div>
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="D">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">D.</span> An exception, because the IDE handled it before the program ran.</div>
    </div>
    <button class="apcs-btn apcs-ex-check">Check answer</button>
    <div class="apcs-ex-feedback">
      <strong>B.</strong> The defining feature is that the program never ran. The IDE underlined a line in red and refused to compile, which is what happens with a syntax error. A is wrong because logic errors only show up after the program runs and produces wrong output. C is wrong because run-time errors happen during execution, not before it starts. D is wrong because exceptions are a specific kind of run-time error, again something that surfaces while the program is executing.
    </div>
  </div>

  <h3>Part B: Identify Sara’s second error</h3>
  <div class="apcs-ex" data-type="mcq" data-answer="A">
    <div class="apcs-ex-stem">After Sara fixed her first error, the program ran, printed six names, and then crashed with <code>NullPointerException</code>. Which classification best describes this second error?</div>
    <div class="apcs-predict-gate">Predict first: the compiler accepted this code, but execution stopped mid-program. Which category fits?</div>
    <div class="apcs-ex-options">
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="A">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">A.</span> An exception, which is a type of run-time error caused by an unexpected condition the compiler could not detect.</div>
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="B">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">B.</span> A logic error, because the program ran for a while and then stopped.</div>
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="C">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">C.</span> A syntax error, because the compiler should have caught it before execution.</div>
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="D">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">D.</span> A compilation warning, because the IDE permitted the program to start but then halted it.</div>
    </div>
    <button class="apcs-btn apcs-ex-check">Check answer</button>
    <div class="apcs-ex-feedback">
      <strong>A.</strong> <code>NullPointerException</code> is a specific type of run-time error caused by an unexpected condition (a null value being used where an object was expected) that the compiler could not detect in advance. Every exception is a run-time error. B is wrong because a logic error means wrong output, not a crash. C is wrong because the compiler does not detect this kind of problem; the code is syntactically valid. D is wrong because Java does not have a notion of a “compilation warning” that halts execution mid-program.
    </div>
  </div>

  <h3>Part C: Structured response</h3>
  <p>In three to five sentences, explain to Mr. Ramirez why Jordan’s final program still has a problem, even though it now compiles and runs to completion without crashing. Identify what type of error this is, and explain how Jordan would have to track it down, since the compiler and the run-time will not flag it for him.</p>

  <div class="mastery-rubric">
    <h4>Scoring rubric</h4>
    <div class="rubric-row">
      <span>Correctly identifies the “every name printed twice” bug as a <strong>logic error</strong>.</span>
      <span class="rubric-score">Full 1 pt</span>
    </div>
    <div class="rubric-row">
      <span>Explains that the program compiles and runs to completion, so neither the compiler nor the run-time flags it.</span>
      <span class="rubric-score">Full 1 pt</span>

    <div class="rubric-row">
      <span>States that the only way to find it is by testing with specific inputs and comparing actual output to expected output.</span>

      <span>Calls the bug a syntax error, run-time error, or exception.</span>
      <span class="rubric-score zero">Zero 0 pt</span>

  <div style="margin-top: 18px !important; padding: 16px 18px !important; background: #1e293b !important; border-radius: 8px !important; border: 1px solid #334155 !important;">
    <h4 style="color: #fbbf24 !important; -webkit-text-fill-color: #fbbf24 !important; margin-top: 0 !important;">Sample full-credit response</h4>
    <p>Jordan’s program is hitting a logic error. The code compiles, so it is not a syntax error, and the program runs to completion without crashing, so it is not a run-time error or exception. The bug is in the algorithm itself, somewhere in the code Jordan is processing each name twice (perhaps an extra loop or a duplicate print statement). Because neither the compiler nor the Java run-time can know what output Mr. Ramirez expected, no automatic tool will flag this. Jordan has to test the program with a known input file, compare the printed list to the names actually in the file, and trace through his code line by line to find where the duplication happens.</p>

<h2>Common AP exam traps</h2>
<p>The exam predictably tests these same misconceptions year after year. Recognize them now and you’ll catch them in May.</p>
<div class="apcsa-traps">
  <div class="apcsa-trap-card">
    <h4>Trap 1: “If it compiles, it works”</h4>
    <p>Successful compilation means the code follows Java’s rules, nothing more. A compiled program can still throw exceptions at run time or produce completely wrong output. The compiler is one layer of error detection, not the only layer.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="apcsa-trap-card">
    <h4>Trap 2: Confusing exception with run-time error</h4>
    <p>Students often treat “exception” and “run-time error” as synonyms. An exception is a <em>specific kind</em> of run-time error caused by an unexpected condition the compiler did not detect. All exceptions are run-time errors, but not all run-time errors are exceptions.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="apcsa-trap-card">
    <h4>Trap 3: Logic errors classified as something else</h4>
    <p>If a program compiles, runs to completion, and produces wrong output, it is still a logic error, even when the wrong output seems “weird” or “unexpected.” The exam will phrase the scenario in ways that tempt you to call it an exception. Don’t.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="apcsa-trap-card">
    <h4>Trap 4: “An algorithm has to be in code”</h4>
    <p>The CED explicitly lists written language and diagrams as valid algorithm representations. A flowchart, a numbered list of steps, and a Java method are all algorithms; the form of representation has nothing to do with whether the algorithm is correct.</p>
  </div>
</div>

<section class="apcsa-extension">
  <span class="ext-badge">Tier 4 · Beyond AP (Optional)</span>
  <h3>How real compilers find more than just syntax errors</h3>
  <p>Modern compilers and IDEs go well beyond the bare minimum the AP exam describes. Java’s compiler also performs <em>type checking</em> (catching mismatches like assigning a <code>String</code> to an <code>int</code>) and <em>definite assignment analysis</em> (refusing to compile if a local variable might be used before it’s assigned). IntelliJ and Eclipse add static analysis on top of that, flagging suspicious patterns, unused variables, methods that always return the same value, possible null dereferences, before you even hit Run. Some of these warnings catch genuine logic errors before they ever execute. None of this is on the AP exam, but it’s worth knowing that the line between “compile-time” and “run-time” is blurrier in professional tools than the CED’s clean four-category framework suggests.</p>

<h2>What is a variable, and why do we need types?</h2>
<p>
  A program that just prints “Hello, World” isn’t very useful. Real programs work with data, test scores, prices, names, true/false flags, and that data has to live somewhere while the program runs. That somewhere is a <strong>variable</strong>: a named storage location that holds a value, where the value can change as the program executes.
</p>

<div class="apcsa-callout concept">
  <h4>Definition</h4>
  <p>A <strong>variable</strong> is a storage location that holds a value, which can change while the program is running. Every variable has a <em>name</em> and an associated <em>data type</em>. A variable of a primitive type holds a primitive value from that type.</p>
</div>

<p>
  Naming a storage location is only half the picture. Java is a <em>statically typed</em> language, which means every variable also has a fixed data type that the compiler tracks. The data type tells Java two things: what set of values can be stored there, and what operations are allowed on those values. Storing the number <code>42</code> behaves very differently from storing the text <code>"42"</code>, one is an integer you can do arithmetic on, the other is a string of characters.
</p>

<h3>The two categories: primitive vs. reference</h3>
<p>
  Java divides every data type into one of two categories. <strong>Primitive types</strong> directly hold simple values like numbers and Boolean truth values. <strong>Reference types</strong> are used to define objects, things like <code>String</code>, <code>Scanner</code>, and any class you write yourself. The CED is explicit about this distinction because it’s the foundation for everything you’ll learn about objects in Unit 1, classes in Unit 3, and collections in Unit 4.
</p>
<p>
  For now, the important thing is that primitives hold the value <em>itself</em>, while references hold a way to find an object that lives elsewhere in memory. In Lesson 1.2 we work entirely with primitives. Reference types come in lesson 1.5 when you create your first <code>String</code> object.
</p>

<div class="apcsa-callout warning">
  <h4>Exclusion statement: AP exam scope</h4>
  <p>The AP Computer Science A course and exam uses only three primitive types: <code>int</code>, <code>double</code>, and <code>boolean</code>. The other five Java primitives, <code>long</code>, <code>short</code>, <code>byte</code>, <code>float</code>, and <code>char</code>, are explicitly excluded from the AP CSA exam. If you see any of those five in an answer choice, the choice is wrong by definition of the course scope.</p>
</div>

<h3>The three primitive types in AP CSA</h3>
<p>Each of the three has a specific job, defined by what values it can hold:</p>
<ul>
  <li>
<strong><code>int</code></strong>. Stores an integer (a whole number, positive, negative, or zero). Examples: <code>0</code>, <code>42</code>, <code>-7</code>, <code>1000000</code>. The <code>int</code> type cannot store decimals.</li>
  <li>
<strong><code>double</code></strong>. Stores a real number, including decimals. Examples: <code>3.14</code>, <code>-0.5</code>, <code>2.0</code>, <code>99.99</code>. Use <code>double</code> any time the value has a fractional part or could need one.</li>
  <li>
<strong><code>boolean</code></strong>. Stores exactly one of two values: <code>true</code> or <code>false</code>. No quotes, no capitals. Use <code>boolean</code> for yes/no flags, on/off states, and the result of comparisons.</li>
</ul>

<div class="apcsa-callout example">
  <h4>Example: picking the right type</h4>
  <p>A program that tracks how many students are in a classroom should use <code>int</code> because you cannot have 24.5 students. A program that tracks the average exam grade should use <code>double</code>. The average of 87, 91, and 95 is 91.0, but the average of 87, 90, and 92 is 89.666..., which an <code>int</code> would truncate to 89. A program that tracks whether the lights in the building are on should use <code>boolean</code>; the lights are either on or off, nothing in between.</p>
</div>

<h3>Declaring variables: the syntax</h3>
<p>
  To declare a variable in Java, you write the data type, then the variable name, optionally followed by <code>=</code> and an initial value, and finally a semicolon. The pattern is:
</p>
<pre><code>dataType variableName = initialValue;</code></pre>
<p>
  Concrete examples that follow the AP CSA scope:
</p>
<pre><code>int score = 0;
double price = 19.99;
boolean isPassing = true;</code></pre>
<p>
  You can also declare a variable without giving it an initial value, <code>int score;</code> is legal, but the variable then has no usable value, and Java will refuse to let you use it in an expression until you assign one. This is called <em>definite assignment</em>, and on the AP exam any code that reads from an uninitialized local variable is a syntax/compile error.
</p>

<h3>Variable naming rules</h3>
<p>
  Java imposes a small set of rules for variable names. They are not optional, breaking them produces a syntax error and the compiler refuses to compile the program:
</p>
<ul>
  <li>Must start with a letter, an underscore (<code>_</code>), or a dollar sign (<code>$</code>), never a digit.</li>
  <li>After the first character, can contain letters, digits, underscores, and dollar signs.</li>
  <li>Cannot be a Java reserved word (<code>int</code>, <code>double</code>, <code>boolean</code>, <code>class</code>, <code>if</code>, etc.).</li>
  <li>Case sensitive: <code>score</code> and <code>Score</code> are two different variables.</li>
  <li>Convention (not a rule, but expected on the exam): use <em>camelCase</em>. The first word is lowercase; subsequent words start with a capital letter. So <code>numStudents</code>, not <code>num_students</code> or <code>NumStudents</code>.</li>
</ul>

<div class="apcsa-callout key-insight">
  <h4>Key insight</h4>
  <p>The data type a programmer chooses is a <em>design decision</em>, not a Java decision. Java will happily let you store the number of students in a <code>double</code>, the program compiles and runs. But on the AP exam, “which is the most appropriate data type” questions have one right answer: the type that exactly matches the values the specification allows. Whole-number quantities use <code>int</code>. Quantities with fractional parts use <code>double</code>. Yes/no states use <code>boolean</code>. Picking a wider type “just in case” is wrong on the exam, even though it might be reasonable engineering elsewhere.</p>
</div>

    hintBtn.onclick = function() {

    };

    if (cm.getOption('lineWrapping')) { wrapBtn.className = 'csa-ce-wrapbtn on'; wrapBtn.innerHTML = 'Wrap: on'; }
    wrapBtn.onclick = function() {
      var on = !cm.getOption('lineWrapping');

      wrapBtn.innerHTML = on ? 'Wrap: on' : 'Wrap lines';
      cm.refresh();
    };

    resetBtn.onclick = function() {
      cm.setValue(p.starter);
      out.className = 'csa-ce-output';
      out.textContent = '';
    };

    runBtn.onclick = function() {
      var code = cm.getValue();
      var wrap = document.getElementById('csa-ce-wrap');
      var lessonId = wrap ? (wrap.getAttribute('data-lesson-id') || '') : '';
      if (CSACE_RUNS >= CSACE_RUN_CAP) {
        out.className = 'csa-ce-output show err';
        out.textContent = 'Run limit reached for this page. Refresh to keep practicing.';
        return;
      }
      CSACE_RUNS++;
      runBtn.disabled = true;
      status.textContent = 'Compiling and running...';
      out.className = 'csa-ce-output';
      out.textContent = '';

      nativeFetch(PROXY_URL, {
        method: 'POST',
        headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
        body: JSON.stringify({ code: code, lessonId: lessonId, problemId: p.id })
      })
      .then(function(res) {
        return res.json().then(function(data) {
          return { ok: res.ok, status: res.status, data: data };
        });
      })
      .then(function(result) {
        setTimeout(function(){ runBtn.disabled = false; }, CSACE_COOLDOWN_MS);
        status.textContent = '';
        var data = result.data;

        if (!result.ok) {
          out.className = 'csa-ce-output show err';
          out.textContent = data.message || 'Run failed. Try again.';
          return;
        }

        if (data.compile_output) {
          out.className = 'csa-ce-output show err';
          out.textContent = 'Compile error:\n' + data.compile_output;
          return;
        }

        if (data.stderr) {
          out.className = 'csa-ce-output show err';
          out.textContent = 'Runtime error:\n' + data.stderr;
          return;
        }

        var stdout = data.stdout || '';

        if (p.expected === null || p.expected === undefined) {
          out.className = 'csa-ce-output show plain';
          out.textContent = 'Output:\n' + (stdout || '(no output)');
          return;
        }

        if (normalize(stdout) === normalize(p.expected)) {
          out.className = 'csa-ce-output show ok';
          if (window.APCS_reportAttempt) { APCS_reportAttempt({ item_id: lessonId + '-code-1', item_type: 'cfu', score: 1, max_score: 1, detail: [{ q: idx + 1, sel: null, ok: true }] }); }
          out.textContent = '✓ Correct!\nOutput: ' + stdout.replace(/\n$/, '');
        } else {
          out.className = 'csa-ce-output show err';
          out.textContent = '✗ Not quite.\nYour output: ' + (stdout.replace(/\n$/, '') || '(none)') + '\nExpected: ' + p.expected;
        }
      })
      .catch(function(err) {
        setTimeout(function(){ runBtn.disabled = false; }, CSACE_COOLDOWN_MS);
        status.textContent = '';
        out.className = 'csa-ce-output show err';
        out.textContent = 'Could not reach the code runner. Check your connection and try again.';
      });
    };
  }

  function init() {
    for (var i = 0; i < CSACE_PROBLEMS.length; i++) {
      buildProblem(CSACE_PROBLEMS[i], i);
    }
  }

  if (document.readyState === 'loading') {
    document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', init);
  } else {
    init();
  }
})();
</script>

  <span class="mastery-badge">Tier 3 · AP Mastery Challenge</span>
  <h2>The Library Checkout System</h2>
  <p>Mr. Chen’s computer science class is designing a small library checkout system. The program needs to track, for each book: the book’s ID number (whole numbers from 1 up to several thousand), the late fee owed on the book (which can include cents), and whether the book is currently checked out. One student suggests declaring the variables this way, all in their <code>main</code> method:</p>
  <pre><code>double bookId = 4271.0;
int lateFee = 2.50;
boolean isCheckedOut = "true";</code></pre>
  <p>Mr. Chen looks at the declarations and tells the student that two of the three will not compile, and the third compiles but uses an inappropriate type for the AP CSA design standard.</p>

  <h3>Part A: Which declaration is technically valid but uses the wrong type?</h3>
  <div class="apcs-ex" data-type="mcq" data-answer="A">
    <div class="apcs-ex-stem">Which of the three declarations compiles successfully but uses an inappropriate data type for what the value represents?</div>
    <div class="apcs-predict-gate">Predict first: which line has correct syntax but the wrong type-to-value match?</div>
    <div class="apcs-ex-options">
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="A">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">A.</span> <code>double bookId = 4271.0;</code> compiles, but a book ID is a whole number, so <code>int</code> is the appropriate type.</div>
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="B">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">B.</span> <code>int lateFee = 2.50;</code> compiles, but should use <code>double</code> for clarity.</div>
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="C">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">C.</span> <code>boolean isCheckedOut = "true";</code> compiles, but Boolean values shouldn’t be in quotes.</div>
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="D">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">D.</span> None of them compile.</div>
    </div>
    <button class="apcs-btn apcs-ex-check">Check answer</button>
    <div class="apcs-ex-feedback">
      <strong>A.</strong> <code>double bookId = 4271.0;</code> is the one that compiles but uses the wrong type. The syntax is valid Java, but a book ID is always a whole number, so the appropriate AP CSA type is <code>int</code>. B is wrong because <code>int lateFee = 2.50;</code> does not compile at all (decimal value into an int variable). C is wrong because <code>"true"</code> is a String literal, not a Boolean, so that declaration also fails to compile. D is wrong because option A does compile.
    </div>
  </div>

  <h3>Part B: Which declaration has a clear syntax error?</h3>
  <div class="apcs-ex" data-type="mcq" data-answer="B">
    <div class="apcs-ex-stem">Which declaration produces a compile error because the value on the right side does not match the declared type?</div>
    <div class="apcs-predict-gate">Predict first: Java is statically typed, so the compiler checks that the value matches the type. Which line breaks that rule most clearly?</div>
    <div class="apcs-ex-options">
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="A">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">A.</span> <code>double bookId = 4271.0;</code>
</div>
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="B">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">B.</span> <code>int lateFee = 2.50;</code> (storing a decimal value into an <code>int</code> variable).</div>
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="C">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">C.</span> <code>boolean isCheckedOut = "true";</code>
</div>
      <div class="apcs-opt" data-letter="D">
<span class="apcs-opt-letter">D.</span> Both B and C produce compile errors for type mismatch.</div>
    </div>
    <button class="apcs-btn apcs-ex-check">Check answer</button>
    <div class="apcs-ex-feedback">
      <strong>B.</strong> <code>int lateFee = 2.50;</code> is the clearest type-mismatch error: the right side is a <code>double</code> literal (2.50) and the variable is declared <code>int</code>. Java refuses to implicitly narrow a <code>double</code> to an <code>int</code>. A is wrong because <code>double bookId = 4271.0;</code> is perfectly valid syntax (a <code>double</code> can hold 4271.0). C also fails to compile, but D over-claims: while C does have a type mismatch, the question asks for the clearest single example, and only one answer can be correct in standard AP MCQ format.
    </div>
  </div>

  <h3>Part C: Structured response</h3>
  <p>In four to six sentences, rewrite all three declarations correctly so they compile and use the most appropriate AP CSA primitive type for what each value represents. Then explain in one or two sentences why a <code>String</code> in quotes (like <code>"true"</code>) is not the same as the Boolean value <code>true</code> in Java, even though they look similar.</p>

    <p>The corrected declarations are: <code>int bookId = 4271;</code> because book IDs are whole numbers; <code>double lateFee = 2.50;</code> because a late fee can have cents; and <code>boolean isCheckedOut = true;</code> because checkout status is exactly true or false. <h2>Common AP exam traps</h2>
<p>The exam tests these same mistakes year after year. Spotting them in May starts with recognizing them now.</p>
<div class="apcsa-traps">
  <div class="apcsa-trap-card">
    <h4>Trap 1: Out-of-scope primitives as distractors</h4>
    <p>Answer choices that mention <code>long</code>, <code>short</code>, <code>byte</code>, <code>float</code>, or <code>char</code> are <em>always wrong</em> on the AP CSA exam by definition of course scope. If you see them, eliminate them immediately. The only correct primitives are <code>int</code>, <code>double</code>, and <code>boolean</code>.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="apcsa-trap-card">
    <h4>Trap 2: Storing decimals in <code>int</code>
</h4>
    <p>An assignment like <code>int x = 2.5;</code> does <em>not</em> compile. Java refuses to assign a <code>double</code> value to an <code>int</code> variable without explicit conversion (covered in Lesson 1.3). The compiler reports a type mismatch error.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="apcsa-trap-card">
    <h4>Trap 3: Confusing <code>"true"</code> with <code>true</code>
</h4>
    <p>A Boolean literal is <code>true</code> or <code>false</code>, lowercase, no quotes. Quoting them turns them into <code>String</code> values, which cannot be assigned to a <code>boolean</code> variable. The exam tests this directly.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="apcsa-trap-card">
    <h4>Trap 4: Variable names that start with a digit</h4>
    <p><code>int 1stPlace</code> is a syntax error. The first character must be a letter, an underscore, or a dollar sign. <code>place1</code> and <code>firstPlace</code> are valid; <code>1stPlace</code> is not.</p>
  </div>
</div>

<section class="apcsa-extension">
  <span class="ext-badge">Tier 4 · Beyond AP (Optional)</span>
  <h3>Why money is usually <em>not</em> stored as <code>double</code> in real systems</h3>
  <p>The AP exam expects <code>double</code> for any quantity with a decimal part, including money. In real production systems, though, financial software almost never uses <code>double</code> for money. The reason is that <code>double</code> stores values in binary floating-point format, which cannot exactly represent simple decimals like 0.1. Adding 0.1 + 0.2 in Java produces 0.30000000000000004, close, but not exact. Over millions of transactions, those rounding errors compound. Real banking software uses arbitrary-precision decimal types (Java’s <code>BigDecimal</code>, or in some languages a dedicated “money” type) that store the digits exactly. This is beyond the AP CSA scope, but it’s worth knowing that “the most appropriate type on the exam” and “the most appropriate type in industry” are not always the same answer.</p>

<h2>Privacy Risks of Storing Personal Data (4.1.A)</h2>

<p>Every time a program stores data about a user, it creates a potential privacy risk. The 
AP CSA exam expects you to be able to <strong>identify what constitutes PII</strong>, explain <strong>why storing it creates risk</strong>, and recognize when combining non-PII data creates a new privacy problem.</p>

<h3>What Is PII?</h3>
<p>PII is any data that, alone or combined with other data, can identify a specific person. Examples include:</p>
<ul>
  <li>Name, address, phone number, email</li>
  <li>Social Security number, driver's license, passport number</li>
  <li>Biometric data (fingerprints, face scans)</li>
  <li>IP address, GPS coordinates, device identifiers</li>
  <li>Medical and financial records</li>
</ul>

<div class="apcsa-callout concept">
  <h4>📌n The Aggregation Problem</h4>
  <p>Each of the following alone seems harmless: your first name, the city you live in, the college you attended, your employer. But combined, they likely identify you uniquely. This is <strong>data aggregation</strong> — one of the most commonly tested concepts in this topic on the AP exam.</p>
</div>

<h3>Why Stored Data Creates Risk</h3>
<p>Stored data can be breached, sold, subpoenaed, or used in ways users didn't anticipate. Key risks the AP exam focuses on:</p>
<ul>
  <li>
<strong>Data breaches:</strong> Unauthorized access exposes stored PII.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Re-identification:</strong> Anonymized data can be de-anonymized when combined with other public data.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Surveillance:</strong> Governments or corporations can track behavior using digital footprints.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Purpose creep:</strong> Data collected for one reason is later used for another without consent.</li>
</ul>

<div class="apcsa-callout trap">
  <h4>⚠️ AP Exam Trap: Legal ≠ Ethical</h4>
  <p>The AP exam frequently tests whether students can distinguish between what is <em>legal</em> and what is <em>ethical</em>. A company can legally collect and sell your browsing history in many jurisdictions — but that doesn't make it ethical. Watch for MCQ answer choices that conflate the two.</p>
</div>

<!-- ==================== SECTION 2 ==================== -->
<h2>Data Quality and Bias (4.1.B)</h2>

<p>When a data set is biased, any algorithm trained on it or run against it will produce biased results — even if the code is written perfectly. Recognizing bias is a software design skill, not just a social awareness skill.</p>

<h3>Types of Bias in Data</h3>
<ul>
  <li>
<strong>Representation bias:</strong> The data set underrepresents some groups. A facial recognition model trained mostly on light-skinned faces performs poorly on darker-skinned faces.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Historical bias:</strong> Past data encodes past discrimination. A hiring algorithm trained on historical résumés may perpetuate the same patterns.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Measurement bias:</strong> The tool used to collect data is inaccurate for some groups. A sensor calibrated for one demographic may give systematically wrong reading
s for another.</li>
  <li>
<strong>Feedback loop bias:</strong> An algorithm's decisions create more data that reinforces its original bias.</li>
</ul>

<div class="apcsa-callout example">
  <h4>✅ Example: Biased Training Data</h4>
  <p>A loan-approval algorithm is trained on 10 years of historical approvals. Because past practices denied loans to certain zip codes, the algorithm learns to penalize those zip codes — even if race is not an explicit variable. The data quality problem (biased historical decisions) produces a biased algorithm.</p>
</div>

<h3>Data Quality Factors</h3>
<p>Beyond bias, data quality also depends on:</p>
<ul>
  <li>
<strong>Accuracy:</strong> Does the data correctly reflect reality?</li>
  <li>
<strong>Completeness:</strong> Are there missing values that skew results?</li>
  <li>
<strong>Timeliness:</strong> Is the data current enough for the use case?</li>
  <li>
<strong>Consistency:</strong> Is data collected the same way across all records?</li>
</ul>

<!-- ==================== REAL WORLD ==================== -->
<h2>Real-World Connection</h2>

<div class="apcsa-callout concept">
  <h4>📌 Why This Section Opens Unit 4</h4>
  <p>Unit 4 is about arrays, ArrayLists, searching, sorting, and algorithms — powerful tools for processing data at scale. Topic 4.1 comes first to establish a principle: <strong>what you do with data has consequences</strong>. Every array you process in this unit could represent real people. The AP exam tests whether future programmers think about that before they write the loop.</p>
</div>

<h3>The Programmer's Responsibility</h3>
<p>When you write code that collects, stores, or processes user data, you take on ethical obligations:</p>
<ul>
  <li>Collect only what you need (data minimization).</li>
  <li>Be transparent about what data is collected and why.</li>
  <li>Secure stored data appropriately.</li>
  <li>Examine training data for bias before deploying algorithms.</li>
  <li>Consider who might be harmed by your program's outputs.</li>
</ul>

<!-- ==================== SUMMARY ==================== -->
<h2>Summary</h2>
<ul>
  <li>PII is any data that can identify a specific individual; combining non-PII data can also create PII through aggregation.</li>
  <li>Storing personal data creates risks: breaches, re-identification, surveillance, and purpose creep.</li>
  <li>Legal data practices are not automatically ethical — the AP exam tests this distinction explicitly.</li>
  <li>Biased data produces biased algorithms; types include representation, historical, measurement, and feedback loop bias.</li>
  <li>Programmers share responsibility for the ethical use of data their code handles.</li>
</ul>

Social Engineering Tactics: Intimidation vs Urgency (Examples & How to Spot Them)

Intimidation and urgency are the two psychological tactics the AP Cybersecurity framework names for social engineering. Intimidation pressures you with the threat of a consequence; urgency pressures you with a deadline. The exam shows you a message and asks which tactic is primary.

Contents

  1. The two tactics
  2. Why these tactics work
  3. Real-world example
  4. Key terms
  5. Match it up
  6. Check for Understanding
  7. FAQ
2framework tactics (EK 1.1.A.2)
Threat= intimidation
Deadline= urgency
The two framework tactics: a threat (intimidation) vs a clock (urgency).

The two tactics

Intimidation threatens a negative consequence if the target does not comply, such as losing access, being fined, or being reported (EK 1.1.A.2). It works by triggering a natural aversion to harm, so fear pushes the target to act (EK 1.1.B.2).

Urgency invents a reason the target must act immediately, such as a short countdown or a closing window (EK 1.1.A.2). It works by triggering a fast reaction to time pressure, which prevents the target from stopping to check whether the request is reasonable (EK 1.1.B.3).

Scenario

A message reads: 'Your account shows illegal activity. Verify now or it will be reported to authorities.' Which tactic is primary?

Reveal answer

Intimidation. The core lever is the threatened consequence (being reported). The word 'now' adds urgency, but the message leans on fear of a negative outcome.

Exam tip

Most real messages use both. The question asks for the PRIMARY tactic. Ask one thing: is the pressure a threat (intimidation) or a clock (urgency)?

Why these tactics work

Both tactics rely on common psychological principles that influence behavior (EK 1.1.B.1). They short-circuit careful thinking, just in different ways.

Intimidation hijacks fear: people avoid threatened losses quickly. Urgency hijacks reflex: people rush time-sensitive tasks and skip the safety check they would normally run.

Scenario

'Congratulations, you won a gift card. Claim it in the next 10 minutes.' Which tactic is primary?

Reveal answer

Urgency. A reward paired with a short deadline is time pressure, not a threat. There is no negative consequence, so it is not intimidation.

Real-world example

Government-impersonation scam calls

The FTC has warned for years about calls claiming to be the IRS or police that threaten arrest or fines unless you pay that same day. The threatened consequence is intimidation; the same-day deadline adds urgency.

Primary tactic: intimidation, with urgency layered on top.

Key Terms

Social engineering Manipulating a person into revealing information or taking an unsafe action.
Intimidation Threatening a negative consequence to force compliance.
Urgency Creating time pressure so the target acts before thinking.
Elicitation Drawing sensitive information out of a target through conversation.

Common Mistakes

!

Calling any deadline 'intimidation'

A countdown with no threatened consequence is urgency. Intimidation requires a threatened loss.

!

Treating the tactic as the impact

Intimidation is a tactic. The impacts are what the attacker gains: personal information, credentials, or malware.

!

Assuming only one tactic is present

Real messages often mix both. Identify the dominant lever, not the only one.

!

Reading a reward as intimidation

A prize with a deadline is urgency. Intimidation needs a threatened negative outcome.

B. The one-hour clock is the dominant pressure (urgency); the suspension is a mild threat. Both appear, urgency leads.

D. The core lever is the threatened arrest, a negative consequence, which is intimidation. 'Today' adds urgency but the message leans on fear.
Question 3

A. Urgency is time pressure that prevents the target from pausing to verify (EK 1.1.B.3).

C. A reward with a short deadline is urgency. No threatened consequence is present, so it is not intimidation.
Question 5

B. I and II describe intimidation. Rewards belong to other lures, so III is false.
